etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the phrase jobbe of work (“piece of work”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a variant of Middle English gobbe (“mass, lump”); or perhaps related to Middle English jobben (“to jab, thrust, peck”), or Middle English choppe (“piece, bargain”). More at gob, jab, chop.

definitions.definition: A task.

quote.text: And it's my job to take care of the skanks on the road that you bang.

definitions.definition: An economic role for which a person is paid.

quote.citation: 1984, Johnny Marr & Morrissey (lyrics and music), “Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now”, in Hatful of Hollow, performed by The Smiths:
quote.text: I was looking for a job and then I found a job / And heaven knows I'm miserable now

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, Schumpeter, “Cronies and capitols”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: Policing the relationship between government and business in a free society is difficult. Businesspeople have every right to lobby governments, and civil servants to take jobs in the private sector.

Here I am at my new job!
Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: (in noun compounds) Plastic surgery.
(in noun compounds) A sex act.

quote.citation: 2000 August 6, “Easy Come, Easy Go”, in Sex and the City, season 3, episode 9, spoken by Samantha:
quote.text: You men have no idea what we're dealing with down there. Teeth placement, and jaw stress, and suction, and gag reflex, and all the while bobbing up and down, moaning and trying to breathe through our noses. Easy? Honey, they don't call it a job for nothing.

definitions.definition: (computing) A task, or series of tasks, carried out in batch mode (especially on a mainframe computer).
A public transaction done for private profit; something performed ostensibly as a part of official duty, but really for private gain; a corrupt official business.
(informal) A robbery or heist.

quote.citation: 2010, J. Lamar, Honor, Deception and Justice, page 53:
quote.text: This freak Vernon got the intelligence on the safe job and passed it on to some other freak, a guy that hears voices in his head and talks back to them.  […]  We don't think [Vernon's squeeze] is in on the heist, but she apparently is in love with this creep who is laying the pipe in her trough!

definitions.definition: Any affair or event which affects one, whether fortunately or unfortunately.
(colloquial) A thing or whatsit (often used in a vague way to refer to something whose name one cannot recall).

quote.citation: 1936, Proceedings of the annual meeting of the American Warehousemen's Association, volume 45, page 376:
quote.text: One of them was about nine years ago when I stood in white tie and tails beside a little blonde job (laughter and applause) down in front of the First Methodist Church of Birmingham,  […]

definitions.definition: (UK, slang, law enforcement) The police as a profession, act of policing, or an individual police officer.[1]

quote.citation: 2018 February 11, Colin Dexter, Russell Lewis, 14:17 from the start, in Endeavour(Cartouche), season 5, episode 2 (TV series), spoken by DS Endeavour Morse (Shaun Evans):
quote.text: “He was ex-job, Beavis. Detective sergeant out of County, Banbury, retired in ‘59.”

quote.citation: 2018 July 24, Chris Merritt, Last Witness:A Gripping Crime Thriller You Won’t Be Able To Put Down:
quote.text: But there it was on the screen: The personal details of his old colleague from Kennington station in the late nineties. […] She’s job. We used to work together.

quote.citation: 2022 February 9, Daragh Carville, Richard Clark, Furquan Akhtar, 01:33 from the start, in The Bay, season 3, episode 5, spoken by D.S Jenn Townsend (Marsha Thomason):
quote.text: “I’m job, D.S Townsend. I have to report a missing person.”

definitions.definition: (vulgar, slang) A penis.
(intransitive) To do odd jobs or occasional work for hire.

quote.text: Authors of all work, to job for the season.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To work as a jobber.
(intransitive, professional wrestling slang) To take the loss, usually in a demeaning or submissive manner.
(transitive, trading) To buy and sell for profit, as securities; to speculate in.
(transitive, often with out) To subcontract a project or delivery in small portions to a number of contractors.
(intransitive) To seek private gain under pretence of public service; to turn public matters to private advantage.

quote.text: And judges job, and bishops bite the town.

definitions.definition: To hire or let in periods of service.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  ...and a pair of handsome horses were jobbed, with which Jos drove about in state in the park...

definitions.definition: (intransitive, now rare, regional) To peck (of a bird); (more generally) to poke or prod (at, into). [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a raven pitch'd upon him, and there sate, jobbing of the sore

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pierce or poke (someone or something), typically with a sharp or pointed object; to stab. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1844, Charles Dickens, chapter 33, in Martin Chuzzlewit:
quote.text: He had ‘jobbed out’ the eye of one gentleman.

definitions.definition: (transitive, now Australia) To hit (someone) with a quick, sharp punch; to jab. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 2001, Richard Flanagan, Gould's Book of Fish, Vintage, published 2016, page 40:
quote.text: A stranger jobbed me in the mug so hard that I fell off my chair.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A sudden thrust or stab; a jab or punch. [16th–20th c.]

quote.text: Fair dinkum, a man ought to give you a job in the b— face.
